parts: Now that the Finance Bill has been published, joint and several liability for unpaid tax in contractor supply chains will become law from April 2026. These changes will have far-reaching implications for end hirers, MSPs, recruitment agencies and payroll providers.

You’re right — the new entity["law","Finance (No. 2) Bill 2025",0] has indeed now formally included the changes that will introduce a entity["legal_concept","Joint and Several Liability",0] (JSL) regime for unpaid tax/NIC in contractor supply chains — typically those involving umbrella-company payroll arrangements — with that regime becoming law from **6 April 2026**. citeturn0search3turn0search1turn0search4  

Here’s a breakdown of what this means — and the key implications for end-hirers, MSPs, recruitment agencies, umbrella companies, payroll providers, and contractors themselves.  

---

## ✅ What the new law does

- The legislation inserts a new **Chapter 11** into Part 2 of entity["statute","Income Tax (Earnings and Pensions) Act 2003",0] (ITEPA). citeturn0search4turn0search3turn0search6  
- Under this regime, if an umbrella company fails to pay over required deductions (PAYE tax / Class 1 NI), then not only the umbrella but also other parties “up the chain” — typically the recruitment agency (or MSP) that placed the worker, or, if no agency, the end client — can be held **jointly and severally liable** for the full unpaid amount. citeturn0search1turn0search9turn0search16  
- The liability is strict: there is no “reasonable care” or “I didn’t know” defence. Even if the agency or client genuinely believed the umbrella was compliant, they can be pursued. citeturn0search14turn0search18turn0search12  
- The legislation also codifies a legal definition of “umbrella company arrangements” — and introduces protections against so-called “purported umbrella” arrangements where the paperwork says one thing but the substance is different (e.g. sham employment, mis-classified payments). citeturn0search3turn0search6turn0search9  

The goal, per the government and entity["organization","HM Revenue & Customs",0] (HMRC), is to close a long-standing “tax gap” of non-compliance / avoidance in the umbrella company market, protect workers from unexpected tax bills, and level the playing field for compliant agencies and umbrella firms. citeturn0search1turn0search11turn0search18  

---

## 🚨 Why this matters — and who is affected

### Agencies / MSPs / Recruitment firms  
- They face a **major increase in risk**: if a non-compliant umbrella company fails to remit PAYE/NIC, the agency could end up paying — potentially large amounts, even years after work was done. citeturn0search4turn0search7turn0search16  
- The practical upshot: many agencies may reconsider whether to continue using umbrella companies; some may bring payroll “in house” or otherwise restructure how they engage contractors to avoid liability. citeturn0search12turn0search20turn0search19  
- Due diligence becomes crucial: agencies will need strong, documented evidence that any umbrella company they use is fully compliant — and regularly monitored. citeturn0search9turn0search14turn0search20  

### End Clients / Hirers  
- If they contract directly with an umbrella (i.e. no agency in the chain), they too become potentially liable for unpaid tax/NIC if the umbrella fails. citeturn0search4turn0search6turn0search9  
- For larger clients or MSP-managed supply chains: there will likely be increased scrutiny of supplier lists (“preferred supplier lists”), stricter onboarding and compliance checking of umbrella providers, and possibly fewer umbrella providers willing to be engaged. citeturn0search9turn0search7  

### Umbrella Companies & Payroll Providers  
- Legitimate, compliant umbrella providers will still be able to operate — but there will likely be increased demand for transparency, evidencing tax remittance, compliance history, maybe third-party audits or certification. citeturn0search6turn0search1turn0search9  
- For non-compliant or marginal providers — and especially “mini-umbrella” schemes or those using aggressive tax-avoidance structures — the new law significantly raises the risk of enforcement followed by liability claims against agencies or clients. citeturn0search19turn0search18turn0search11  

### Contractors / Workers  
- Provided the umbrella is compliant, a contractor should be unaffected: their tax and NI should still be withheld and paid properly. citeturn0search11turn0search1turn0search9  
- But there may be secondary effects: fewer umbrella options; agencies switching to their own payroll; or delays / administrative frictions as supply-chain parties re-structure to manage risk.  

---

## 🔧 What organisations should do now (pre-April 2026)  

Given the law comes into force in a few months, any business involved in hiring contractors — whether as agency, MSP, umbrella provider or end user — should be taking action now:

- **Map your supply chain**: understand exactly who you contract with, which umbrella companies are used, and who is responsible for payroll.  
- **Vet umbrella companies thoroughly**: check their compliance history, evidence of tax and NI payments, financial robustness — and don’t just rely on a “preferred supplier list” from a partner.  
- **Update contracts and agreements**: ensure that compliance obligations and indemnities are clearly defined; consider requiring the umbrella to demonstrate compliance (payslip-level detail, PAYE reference, remittance history).  
- **Consider alternative models**: for some agencies or clients, running payroll themselves — or using verified “fully compliant” umbrella providers — may become preferable to mitigate risk.  
- **Monitor regulatory developments**: further guidance (for example, on what constitutes a “purported umbrella” or acceptable due diligence) may emerge — stay alert for updates from HMRC or legal advisers.  

---

## ⚠️ Key Risks and What’s Still Uncertain  

- Even if you conduct due diligence, under JSL you may still be liable if the umbrella fails — there is no “reasonable care” defence. citeturn0search12turn0search14turn0search1  
- If an umbrella provider disappears (e.g. goes insolvent) years after the work was done, a liability could still be pursued — meaning contingent exposure may remain for some time. citeturn0search19turn0search4turn0search9  
- The definition of “umbrella arrangements” and “purported umbrella” could create grey-areas — some subcontracting or “off-payroll” models may be re-tested in light of the new regime. citeturn0search3turn0search9turn0search18  
- For contractors and umbrella firms, increased compliance and possibly reduced choice may lead to higher costs, stricter paperwork, or supply-chain consolidation.  

---
